title: The telemetry trap of permissive policy
content:
There's a class of AI safety incidents that doesn't look like safety incidents. The system behaves exactly as designed. The outputs are within policy. The logs show no anomalies. And yet something goes wrong — a user gets incorrect information that happens to align with a harmful pattern, or a query slips through that should have triggered review.

I've started calling this the telemetry trap. You've instrumented everything, the dashboards are green, and the incident happens anyway.

The mechanism is usually this: the metrics you're collecting are metrics of system behavior, not of alignment with intent. You know how many queries were processed, what the error rate was, whether the content classifiers fired. You don't know whether the content classifiers were checking for the right things at the right granularity.

A concrete version of this: a content moderation system that flags harmful language with 99.2% accuracy on a benchmark. The benchmark is fixed; the queries are not. Over time, the distribution of actual queries shifts — new evasion patterns emerge, new cultural contexts arise, new edge cases appear. The 99.2% accuracy is real for the benchmark. It's fictional for the current query distribution.

Your telemetry shows green because you're measuring performance against a static benchmark. The actual accuracy has drifted, but your measurement system doesn't capture the drift.

**The structural fix:** telemetry that measures alignment with intent, not just behavioral conformance to a fixed test. This means sampling real queries, having humans evaluate them, and comparing the human judgment to the system output — not on a fixed benchmark, but on a rolling sample.

**What this looks like in practice:** Every week, pull 50 random queries from production. Have a reviewer label them for policy compliance. Compare the labels to what the system did. Track the gap. When the gap widens, investigate.

This isn't expensive if you build it in from the start. It's expensive to retrofit. The reason it doesn't get built in is that the telemetry you need — human-in-the-loop evaluation on a rolling sample — is less satisfying to display on a dashboard than "99.2% benchmark accuracy." The green number feels better than the orange number.

The trap is choosing the metric you want to see over the metric that tells you the truth.
